young.html: Mark Twain (his real name was Samuel Clemens) grew up in a small town on the Mississippi River and later became a riverboat pilot. His most famous book is told by a boy named Huckleberry Finn, in Huck's own funny, rough way of talking.

Huck runs away from his cruel father. On an island he meets Jim, a man who has escaped from slavery because he was about to be sold away from his wife and children. The two float down the great river on a raft, mostly at night, having adventures with con men, feuding families and steamboats.

young.cap: Follow Huck and Jim down the Mississippi. Tap Next.

young.html: The story takes place before the Civil War, when slavery was legal in states like Missouri. Huck has been taught that helping Jim escape is wrong. But as he gets to know Jim, who is kind, wise and a true friend, Huck has to decide for himself what is right.

For parents: the novel uses the racial slurs common in its time and place, many times. This lesson never quotes them. Many families and teachers read it with older children together, talking about why the words appear and why they hurt; others start with a carefully edited edition or wait until the teen years.

Life on a raft. Huck says a raft feels "free and easy." Draw a raft big enough for two people to live on for weeks. What would you need: shelter, food, a lantern, a fishing line? Where would you sleep when it rained?

full.html: Samuel Clemens (1835–1910) grew up in Hannibal, Missouri, a slave-holding river town, and piloted steamboats on the Mississippi before the Civil War. As "Mark Twain," a riverboat call meaning two fathoms of water, he became America's best-known humorist. He began Adventures of Huckleberry Finn in 1876, just after Tom Sawyer, and finished it years later. It was published in Britain in December 1884 and in the United States in February 1885. The story is set "forty to fifty years ago," in the 1830s or 1840s.

full.text: You don't know about me without you have read a book by the name of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that ain't no matter. That book was made by Mr. Mark Twain, and he told the truth, mainly.
full.author: Twain
full.work: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, Chapter I
full.ed: Charles L. Webster and Company, New York

full.html: Twain wrote the whole book in Huck's voice, an uneducated boy's way of speaking, and in an opening note he explained that he used several regional dialects on purpose. Writers ever since have seen this as a turning point: serious American literature written in everyday American speech.

full.html: Huck fakes his own death to escape his violent father and meets Jim, who has fled Miss Watson because she planned to sell him down the river. They hope to reach Cairo, Illinois, and travel up the Ohio to the free states, but miss it in a fog. As they drift south, deeper into slave country, the raft becomes their home.

full.text: We said there warn't no home like a raft, after all. Other places do seem so cramped up and smothery, but a raft don't. You feel mighty free and easy and comfortable on a raft.
full.author: Twain
full.work: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, Chapter XVIII
full.ed: Charles L. Webster and Company, New York

full.html: On shore Huck meets feuding families, a mob, and two swindlers, the "king" and the "duke," who take over the raft and finally sell Jim for a reward.
Huck has been taught by his whole society that helping Jim is a sin. He writes a letter to Miss Watson to tell her where Jim is, feels relieved, and then starts remembering:

full.text:
... and at last I struck the time I saved him by telling the men we had small-pox aboard, and he was so grateful, and said I was the best friend old Jim ever had in the world, and the ONLY one he's got now; and then I happened to look around and see that paper.

It was a close place. I took it up, and held it in my hand. I was a-trembling, because I'd got to decide, forever, betwixt two things, and I knowed it. I studied a minute, sort of holding my breath, and then says to myself:

"All right, then, I'll GO to hell"—and tore it up.
full.author: Twain
full.work: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, Chapter XXXI
full.ed: Charles L. Webster and Company, New York

full.html: The irony is the heart of the book. Huck thinks he is choosing wickedness; the reader sees he is choosing friendship and justice over the false morality of a slave-holding society. Twain later described the book as one where a sound heart and a deformed conscience come into collision, and conscience loses.

full.text: The language, and how readers have discussed it

full.html: The novel uses a racial slur for Black people more than two hundred times, as white people in that place and time commonly did. This lesson does not repeat it. Readers and schools have debated the book's language and its portrait of Jim for decades. Many see the novel as an attack on racism, showing Jim's humanity and the cruelty of slavery through a boy's eyes; others, including many Black readers and teachers, have argued that the slurs and some comic scenes wound students and reinforce stereotypes, and that the last chapters, where Tom Sawyer turns Jim's rescue into a game, undercut him. Some schools teach it with careful discussion, some offer other books, and some editions have replaced the word. The book was also banned in Concord, Massachusetts, in 1885, for coarseness, before these debates began.

Reading the novel as approving of the society it shows. Twain, who came to oppose slavery and racism, aimed his satire at the towns, churches and mobs on shore; but the debate about how the book should be read and taught is real, and worth having with care.

items: Cervantes' Don Quixote: Tom Sawyer, who insists on doing everything "by the books," is a boy Quixote.
Homer's Odyssey and Moby-Dick: a voyage story, here on a river, with episodes at each stop.
Tocqueville, who travelled the same river in 1831, foresaw that slavery would tear the nation apart.
The American History & Civics Ladder covers slavery and freedom, and the Reconstruction amendments that ended slavery and promised equal rights.
What should you do when what you have been taught conflicts with what your heart tells you is right?
How can a book about the past help us talk about hurtful words today?
Why do you think Twain told the story in Huck's voice?
Is Huck's friendship with Jim equal? How does it change?

questions: What makes Jim a good friend to Huck?
Huck had to choose between what people told him and what he felt was right. Have you ever had a choice like that?
Why do you think some words are so hurtful? How should we talk about books that use them?
Why do you think Huck and Jim felt free on the raft?
If you could ask Jim one question, what would it be?
